newsitem.title: UK: Trader seems set to take huge cocoa delivery.
newsitem.headline: Trader seems set to take huge cocoa delivery.

text.p: A trader who misread the volatile cocoa futures market may soon have to take delivery of around 300,000 tonnes of the commodity, worth 300 million pounds ($470 million), the largest physical delivery ever done through a London exchange, trade sources said.

The delivery, which amounts to around a third of a harvest of Ivory Coast, the world's major producer, would be the culmination of a five-month long war of nerves over the London September cocoa futures contract.
"He is going to take all of it. His position is so large that he can't get out of it," said one trader. "But the question is what's he going to do with it next."
The previous record delivery at the London Commodity Exchange was around 250,000 tonnes in March 1995. Futures contracts are usually settled in cash.
Market sources say the trader is commodity major Phibro but Phibro has denied this.
The cost of maintaining such a large position against a falling market is so large that the long holder may not have the stamina to drag the show on for much longer, traders said.

In June, a commodity house which had bought large supplies of cocoa was calling the shots when prices rocketed to eight-year highs. Supplies were slow and a large proportion of cocoa beans were failing the grading test.

But things changed. Ivorian crop forecasters changed their tune after an initial scenario of a late harvest, raising the estimate for Ivory Coast to about 900,000 tonnes from 800,000-850,000 in earlier assessments.
"There has been an improvement," said one leading cocoa analyst. "The crop is definitely not going to be late."

This is bad news for the trader, already hit hard by a large tail to the mid-crop this year which enabled the short players, who had sold expecting prices to fall, to muster mountains of cocoa to deliver against September.
A record Ivorian crop has sent prices reeling -- September has sunk to around 955 pounds a tonne from a peak in June of 1,172 -- and the upcoming harvest could increase the jitters.
A timely arrival of the 1996/97 crop would leave the long trader, a net owner, no room for manoeuvre.
But some traders say the jury remains out on the likely repercussions of so much cocoa taken by a single trader.
"Overall he will come out as a loser. But I don't think the game is over yet," said one trader. "Maybe he's got an ace up his sleeve," said another.
Traders said at least some of the September cocoa would be re-appearing in the market, sold against the December and March contracts.

If the Ivorian crop is on time, December delivery could be a more sensible bet since most of the grading certificates expire by the end of the year and regrading would cost a further 1.5 million pounds.
"If you are sitting on a fairly substantial loss, these numbers would begin to become important," said one trader.
If, however, the Ivorian crop is delayed, the long holder could create an artificial shortage by holding the cocoa away from the market.
For the industry, the question is how much cocoa is outside the trader's control. No supply hiccups seem likely, at least in the last quarter of this year, industry sources say.
"We are hearing better and better things (about the crop)," one industry source said. "Our advice is don't buy today but just let the market go."
